newsitem.title: AUSTRIA: IAEA says N.Korea yet to account for plutonium.
newsitem.headline: IAEA says N.Korea yet to account for plutonium.

text.p: North Korea has yet to account for an amount of nuclear-grade plutonium which experts say it possesses and refuses to let inspectors carry out checks at its atomic sites, the U.N. nuclear watchdog said on Tuesday.
The International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) has never been able to confirm that North Korea has a nuclear device but insists it has fissionable material it is not owning up to.

"The agency's position has not changed and the (IAEA) director-general (Hans Blix) has repeated that we still have a discrepancy, that there is more plutonium in this country than has been declared," spokesman Hans-Dietrich Meyer told Reuters.
"We do not know exactly how much, only that there must be more," said Meyer at IAEA headquarters in Vienna.
The leading South Korean newspaper Chosun Ilbo on Tuesday quoted a top Pyongyang defector as saying North Korea could wipe out the capitalist South using nuclear and chemical arms.

The daily published a document it said was written by Hwang Jang-yop, the most senior North Korean official to flee the communist state, saying Pyongyang could turn the South into a "sea of flames" and scorch Japan in a nuclear attack.
The wording was ambiguous and it was not clear whether he was saying North Korea definitely had a nuclear bomb.
Diplomats have urged caution and the IAEA has also taken a cautious stance ever since its dispute with Pyongyang erupted four years ago.

But an inspections report and comments from high-ranking officials raised suspicions that while North Korea may not have gone as far to produce a nuclear device, it had been using fissionable material in a covert nuclear weapons programme.

The IAEA raised international alarm in 1993 when it announced its findings of missing plutonium after the agency's first inspection in North Korea following Pyongyang's agreement to sign the Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty and a safeguards pact with the agency in May 1992.
The IAEA was set up by the United Nations to ensure that countries with nuclear reactors do not use radioactive fuel for military purposes.
Attention focused on a Soviet-designed 50-Megawatt nuclear reactor at the state's main atomic site in Yongbyon, which was closed down temporarily in 1989.
The North Koreans, who have denied any secret nuclear weapons programme, said the shutdown was routine. Experts believe some plutonium may have been extracted and diverted for covert purposes.

The IAEA also called for an immediate inspection of two suspected nuclear waste sites, also at Yongbyon, which could have produced evidence to point to any atomic arms experiments. But Pyongyang refused. U.N. experts can look but cannot touch anything at the site for testing.

To diffuse the nuclear row on the tinderbox Korean peninsula, the United States forged a pact with Pyongyang in 1994 and North Korea froze its old-style graphite-moderated civil nuclear programme. In return, a consortium of states, including South Korea and Japan, have agreed to pay for the construction of safer light-water reactors, which produce little plutonium.

Almost two-thirds of the 8,800 rods from the 50-Megawatt reactor have been put into safe containers, Meyer confirmed. Pyongyang has allowed four IAEA inspectors to observe the operation but, again, will not permit any testing.
"Every step taken which is necessary for safety makes it more difficult and more unlikely that we can ever retrieve the truth," Meyer said.
